items.title: 24.6.2 Separation of Amino Acids by Electrophoresis

source_refs.note: Topic 24.6.2 (PDF 130-131); Figure 24.2 and the ninhydrin equation are redrawn.

blocks.text: Electrophoresis separates the amino acids in a mixture by their charge. A few drops of the mixture are put on a filter paper or gel in a buffered solution between two electrodes. When an electric field is applied, the amino acids separate according to their pI values. If an amino acid's pI is greater than the pH of the solution, it is mostly in a positively charged form and moves towards the cathode; if its pI is lower than the pH, it is mostly negative and moves towards the anode. The greater the difference between pI and pH, the faster it moves. If two amino acids have very similar pI values (such as glycine and leucine), the one with the larger molecular mass moves more slowly, because the charge has to carry a greater mass.

blocks.alt: A yellow strip between a negative electrode on the left and a positive electrode on the right, with three spots: Lysine (pI = 9.74) near the negative end, Alanine (pI = 6.02) in the middle and Glutamic acid (pI = 3.22) near the positive end, each with an arrow from its label.
blocks.caption: Figure 24.2: Separations of amino acids at pH 6 by electrophoresis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 24.2).

blocks.text: Amino acids are colourless, so the spots must be detected. Ninhydrin is used as a locating agent: it reacts with amino acids to give a purple product. Electrophoresis cannot separate large quantities of amino acids; it is used as an analytical method to find how many amino acids a mixture contains. To actually separate a whole mixture, other techniques such as column chromatography are used.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: an amino acid (R and COOH on a carbon carrying NH2) + 2 ninhydrin (a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring with two C=O groups and two OH on the middle carbon), with NaOH over the arrow, gives the purple-colored product (two such ring units joined through C-N=C, each with two C=O) + the by-products H2O, CO2 and RCHO.
blocks.caption: Reaction of an amino acid with ninhydrin (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 131).
